## Challenge: Finding the right Python executable

IDA does not expose which Python interpreter it uses via any config file or queryable API. The `idapyswitch` registry stores a path to `libpython3.X.so` (or `.dylib`/`.dll`), but that library path does not directly tell you the corresponding `python3` executable. For example, when the user wants to use a virtual environment, the `libpython` path might be far removed on the file system. HCLI's only reliable method is to spawn IDA in batch mode (`idat -A -S<script>`) and run a probe script that prints `sys.prefix`, `sys.base_prefix`, `sys.executable`, and related values. Then HCLI runs an 85-line heuristic (`_derive_python_exe`) to work backwards from those values to an actual executable path.

We could parse the IDA registry for this data, but we've avoid this today so that we don't duplicate code and possibly bugs.

Anyways, this probe-and-derive approach is fragile because each platform and Python distribution reports different values.

On Windows, `sys.executable` returns the path to `idat.exe` rather than the Python interpreter ([#133](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/ida-hcli/issues/133)). On macOS with IDA 9.4+, `sys.executable` is also the idat binary. Therefore, HCLI cannot trust this value and must derive the executable from `sys.prefix` using platform-specific path layouts. When `sys.executable` fails and HCLI falls back to searching PATH, but we found that it would find the Windows Store `python3.EXE` shim instead of the Python configured via `idapyswitch` ([#154](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/ida-hcli/issues/154)). HCLI now detects and rejects these shims.

When HCLI itself runs inside a virtual environment (during CI or development), environment variables like `VIRTUAL_ENV`, `PYTHONHOME`, and `PYTHONPATH` leak into the `idat` subprocess, causing IDA to bind to the wrong interpreter ([#178](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/ida-hcli/issues/178)). HCLI now scrubs these variables before launching idat. On macOS, framework Pythons can report the base framework prefix even when running inside a venv, requiring additional validation against known venv roots.

Beyond correctness, the probe is slow. Spawning IDA as a subprocess can take a second or so ([#288](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/ida-hcli/issues/288)). For one-off plugin installs this is tolerable, but if a hypothetical MCP server called `hcli ida python run-script` on every invocation then a multi-second startup penalty is not acceptable. Caching the probe results is risky because IDA stores Python configuration in many places and a stale cache would produce hard-to-debug failures.

The entire probe mechanism also depends on `idat`, the text-mode IDA executable. IDA Home and IDA Free editions don't ship `idat`, so plugin installation fails immediately with `Error: can't find idat` ([#196](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/ida-hcli/issues/196), [#22](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/ida-hcli/issues/22)).

## Challenge: Installing packages into IDA's environment

Even after finding the right Python, HCLI often cannot install packages into it.

Modern Linux distributions (Ubuntu 24.04+, Debian) and some macOS installations mark their system Python with PEP 668's `EXTERNALLY-MANAGED` marker. When IDA uses this system Python (the default on a fresh install), pip refuses to install anything ([#275](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/ida-hcli/issues/275), [#144](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/ida-hcli/issues/144)). Users see `error: externally-managed-environment` and have no idea what to do. Some of them attempt to remove the marker file using admin privileges, but this just delays confusion. Even without PEP 668, some system Python environments live in locations the user cannot write to (`/usr/lib/python3/...`), so `pip install` fails with permission errors.

A separate problem: users who create virtual environments with `uv venv` (without `--seed`) get an environment that has no pip installed ([#124](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/ida-hcli/issues/124)). HCLI detects the correct Python but then fails with `PipNotAvailableError`.

## Challenge: Virtual environment detection gaps

Virtual environments solve the package installation problem, but HCLI has historically struggled to detect them.

A common setup is to activate a venv in `idapythonrc.py`, which runs at IDA startup ([source](https://community.hex-rays.com/t/using-a-virtualenv-for-idapython/261)). But HCLI's batch-mode probe (`idat -A -S<script>`) does not trigger `idapythonrc.py` the same way as interactive IDA (setting `IDA_IS_INTERACTIVE`). The probe sees the base system Python while IDA interactively uses the venv ([#144](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/ida-hcli/issues/144)). Users confirm their venv works in IDA, yet HCLI installs packages into the wrong location.

Until [#279](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/ida-hcli/issues/279), HCLI did not check `IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE` at all, so users who configured their venv via this variable still had HCLI probe idat and find a different Python. Even after that fix, version mismatches go undetected in normal operation: a user can register Python 3.12 with `idapyswitch` but point `IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE` at a Python 3.14 venv. IDA loads `libpython3.12` at startup but the venv's packages are installed for 3.14, producing confusing import failures. HCLI warns about this in `explain-environment` ([#278](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/ida-hcli/issues/278)), but not during normal plugin operations.

A subtler problem: when HCLI is invoked via `uv run --with ida-hcli`, uv creates an ephemeral cache environment and sets `$VIRTUAL_ENV` to point at it, hiding the user's actual venv. HCLI uses three independent heuristics to detect these overlays (path under uv cache dirs, uv-internal ancestor directories, `extends-environment` key in `pyvenv.cfg`).

## Aside: The codebase cost

The complexity of IDA's Python configurability shows up directly in HCLI's codebase. `python.py` (~940 lines) contains the core resolution logic: an 85-line `_derive_python_exe` heuristic with special cases for Windows Store shims, macOS framework Pythons, IDA 9.4+ macOS, and PEP 668 environments, plus a three-level precedence chain in `resolve_current_python` (`$HCLI_CURRENT_IDA_PYTHON_EXE` > `$IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE` > idat probe). `venv.py` (~300 lines) handles virtual environment detection, uv cache discrimination, and version probing. `explain_environment.py` (~700 lines) is a diagnostic command that exists solely because the environment has so many interacting pieces: it probes IDA, checks venvs, validates version consistency, detects PEP 668, warns about uv overlays, and surfaces misconfigurations.

Nearly 2000 lines of code exist to answer the question "which Python does IDA use and can we install packages there?"

## Open questions

A program that uses idalib (IDA as a library) typically has its own virtual environment with its own dependencies. That venv's `site-packages` may not include IDA plugin dependencies, which live in the potentially-separate dedicated IDA virtualenv. How should idalib programs access plugin packages? Options include adding the IDA venv's site-packages to `sys.path`, requiring idalib programs to install plugin deps into their own venv, or having HCLI provide a path helper.

Should HCLI refuse to operate without a venv, or only warn? Refusing would break existing users who have working non-venv setups. Warning is less disruptive but doesn't prevent the support requests.

The setup requires users to create a venv manually. Should HCLI or the IDA installer create one automatically? Auto-creation reduces friction but risks choosing the wrong Python version, location, or permissions.

Even with a shared venv, plugins can have conflicting dependencies. A full solution might require per-plugin virtual environments or a dependency resolver, both much more complex than the current approach.

28	Beyond correctness, the probe is slow. Spawning IDA as a subprocess can take a second or so ([#288](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/ida-hcli/issues/288)). For one-off plugin installs this is tolerable, but if a hypothetical MCP server called `hcli ida python run-script` on every invocation then a multi-second startup penalty is not acceptable. Caching the probe results is risky because IDA stores Python configuration in many places and a stale cache would produce hard-to-debug failures.
29	
30	The entire probe mechanism also depends on `idat`, the text-mode IDA executable. IDA Home and IDA Free editions don't ship `idat`, so plugin installation fails immediately with `Error: can't find idat` ([#196](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/ida-hcli/issues/196), [#22](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/ida-hcli/issues/22)).
31	
32	## Challenge: Installing packages into IDA's environment
33	
34	Even after finding the right Python, HCLI often cannot install packages into it.
35	
36	Modern Linux distributions (Ubuntu 24.04+, Debian) and some macOS installations mark their system Python with PEP 668's `EXTERNALLY-MANAGED` marker. When IDA uses this system Python (the default on a fresh install), pip refuses to install anything ([#275](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/ida-hcli/issues/275), [#144](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/ida-hcli/issues/144)). Users see `error: externally-managed-environment` and have no idea what to do. Some of them attempt to remove the marker file using admin privileges, but this just delays confusion. Even without PEP 668, some system Python environments live in locations the user cannot write to (`/usr/lib/python3/...`), so `pip install` fails with permission errors.
37	
38	A separate problem: users who create virtual environments with `uv venv` (without `--seed`) get an environment that has no pip installed ([#124](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/ida-hcli/issues/124)). HCLI detects the correct Python but then fails with `PipNotAvailableError`.
39	
40	## Challenge: Virtual environment detection gaps
41	
42	Virtual environments solve the package installation problem, but HCLI has historically struggled to detect them.
43	
44	A common setup is to activate a venv in `idapythonrc.py`, which runs at IDA startup ([source](https://community.hex-rays.com/t/using-a-virtualenv-for-idapython/261)). But HCLI's batch-mode probe (`idat -A -S<script>`) does not trigger `idapythonrc.py` the same way as interactive IDA (setting `IDA_IS_INTERACTIVE`). The probe sees the base system Python while IDA interactively uses the venv ([#144](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/ida-hcli/issues/144)). Users confirm their venv works in IDA, yet HCLI installs packages into the wrong location.
45	
46	Until [#279](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/ida-hcli/issues/279), HCLI did not check `IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE` at all, so users who configured their venv via this variable still had HCLI probe idat and find a different Python. Even after that fix, version mismatches go undetected in normal operation: a user can register Python 3.12 with `idapyswitch` but point `IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE` at a Python 3.14 venv. IDA loads `libpython3.12` at startup but the venv's packages are installed for 3.14, producing confusing import failures. HCLI warns about this in `explain-environment` ([#278](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/ida-hcli/issues/278)), but not during normal plugin operations.
47	
48	A subtler problem: when HCLI is invoked via `uv run --with ida-hcli`, uv creates an ephemeral cache environment and sets `$VIRTUAL_ENV` to point at it, hiding the user's actual venv. HCLI uses three independent heuristics to detect these overlays (path under uv cache dirs, uv-internal ancestor directories, `extends-environment` key in `pyvenv.cfg`).
49

1	# All IDAPython Setup Variants
2	
3	Comprehensive catalog of every way a user can configure Python for IDA, based on HCLI source code analysis (python.py, venv.py, explain_environment.py, env.py), community forum posts, and official documentation.
4	
5	## 1. System Python (no venv) — the unmodified default
6	
7	**What the user does:** Installs IDA. Does nothing about Python. On Linux/macOS, IDA picks up whatever system Python is available. On Windows, the installer may bundle Python via `--install_python`.
8	
9	**How HCLI discovers it:** The idat probe runs, reports `sys.prefix == sys.base_prefix` (no venv), `sys.executable` may be `/usr/bin/python3` or `C:\Python3X\python.exe` or even `idat.exe` on Windows. HCLI derives the interpreter from `sys.prefix` using platform-specific path layouts (`bin/python3.X` on POSIX, `Scripts/python.exe` or `python.exe` on Windows).
10	
11	**What breaks:**
12	- PEP 668: On Ubuntu 24.04+, Debian, and some macOS, the system Python is marked `EXTERNALLY-MANAGED` and pip refuses to install anything (#275, #144).
13	- Permission errors: System Python environments may be in read-only locations (`/usr/lib/python3/...`).
14	- Windows Store shims: PATH lookup finds `python3.EXE` in `Microsoft\WindowsApps` which opens the Store instead of running Python (#154). HCLI now detects and rejects these via `_is_windows_store_shim()`.
15	- `sys.executable` is `idat.exe` on Windows (#133) and on macOS IDA 9.4+ — HCLI can't trust it.
16	- No writable environment for plugin dependencies.
17	
18	**Prevalence:** Very common — the default for most users, especially new ones.
19	
20	## 2. Windows bundled Python
21	
22	**What the user does:** Runs the IDA installer on Windows with `--install_python` (or accepts the default to bundle Python 3). IDA ships with a private Python installation in the IDA directory.
23	
24	**How HCLI discovers it:** Same as (1): idat probe finds the bundled interpreter via `sys.prefix`. The path is typically inside the IDA installation directory.
25	
26	**What breaks:**
27	- The bundled Python is not a venv, so it may lack pip or have restricted permissions depending on where IDA is installed (e.g., `C:\Program Files\...`).
28	- No isolation from other IDA installations or system Python.
29	- Users may not realize they have two Pythons (bundled + system) and get confused about which one IDA uses.
30	
31	**Prevalence:** Common on Windows, especially for users who accept installer defaults.
32	
33	## 3. Homebrew / pyenv / Anaconda / system-installed Python via idapyswitch
34	
35	**What the user does:** Installs Python via Homebrew (`brew install python`), pyenv, Anaconda/Miniconda, or python.org installer. Runs `idapyswitch` to point IDA at that Python's `libpython3.X.dylib/.so/.dll`.
36	
37	**How HCLI discovers it:** The idat probe reports the Homebrew/pyenv/Anaconda prefix as `sys.prefix`. HCLI derives the executable from that prefix. IDA 9.4 added detection for uv/anaconda/homebrew Pythons.
38	
39	**What breaks:**
40	- No venv means package installation affects the global environment.
41	- Homebrew Python on macOS may be externally managed (PEP 668).
42	- Anaconda environments add another layer of complexity (conda envs vs. Python venvs).
43	- pyenv shims can confuse PATH-based fallback detection.
44	- macOS framework Pythons report misleading `sys.base_prefix` values, causing HCLI to miss the venv when one is active.
45	
46	**Prevalence:** Common among power users and macOS users.
47	
48	## 4. Virtual environment activated via shell before launching IDA
49	
50	**What the user does:** Creates a venv (`python -m venv ~/.idapro/venv` or `uv venv --seed ~/.idapro/venv`), activates it in the shell (`source ~/.idapro/venv/bin/activate`), then launches IDA from that shell. IDA 9.0+ picks up locally installed modules from the activated venv.
51	
52	**How HCLI discovers it:** The idat probe sees `$VIRTUAL_ENV` set and `sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix`. HCLI's `_derive_python_exe` matches prefix candidates against `$VIRTUAL_ENV` to find the correct interpreter inside the venv.
53	
54	**What breaks:**
55	- Only works when IDA is launched from the activated shell. Doesn't work with desktop shortcuts, file associations, or system launchers.
56	- If HCLI is invoked separately (not from the same activated shell), it won't see `$VIRTUAL_ENV`.
57	- The 9.0 release notes describe this as "simply run IDA from an activated virtual environment" — one sentence, no further guidance.
58	
59	**Prevalence:** Uncommon — inconvenient for daily use, mainly used by developers and CI.
60	
61	## 5. Virtual environment activated via idapythonrc.py
62	
63	**What the user does:** Creates a venv, then adds activation code to `~/.idapro/idapythonrc.py`. The script uses `site.addsitedir()` to add the venv's `site-packages` to `sys.path` and sets `sys.prefix` to the venv root. Runs at every IDA startup.
64	
65	Community-recommended approaches (from https://community.hex-rays.com/t/using-a-virtualenv-for-idapython/261):
66	- Original: Uses `activate_this.py` from the `virtualenv` package (not stdlib `venv`).
67	- Improved (mrexodia): Uses a sentinel flag in `builtins` to prevent re-initialization when switching databases, directly manages site-packages via `site.addsitedir()`.
68	
69	**How HCLI discovers it:** This is where the gap is. HCLI's batch-mode idat probe (`idat -A -S<script>`) does NOT trigger `idapythonrc.py` the same way interactive IDA does (depends on `IDA_IS_INTERACTIVE`). So the probe sees the base system Python while interactive IDA uses the venv (#144). HCLI may install packages into the wrong location.
70	
71	If `$VIRTUAL_ENV` happens to also be set (because the user activated the venv in their shell), HCLI may pick it up from the probe results. But this is unreliable.
72	
73	**What breaks:**
74	- HCLI cannot see the venv — it installs packages into the wrong Python.
75	- `activate_this.py` only exists in `virtualenv`-created envs, not stdlib `venv` or `uv venv`.
76	- Script may execute multiple times per process when opening multiple databases.
77	- `idapythonrc.py` is completely undocumented in official IDA docs.
78	
79	**Prevalence:** Common — the most-recommended community approach before `IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE` existed.
80	
81	## 6. IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE environment variable (recommended)
82	
83	**What the user does:** Creates a venv, then sets `IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE` as a persistent environment variable pointing to the venv's Python interpreter (e.g., `~/.idapro/venv/bin/python3`). Available since IDA 9.1+.
84	
85	**How HCLI discovers it:** `resolve_current_python()` checks `ENV.IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE` as second priority (after `HCLI_CURRENT_IDA_PYTHON_EXE`). If the file exists on disk, returns it immediately — no idat probe needed. Inside the idat probe, `_derive_python_exe` also uses it to validate candidates and as a direct fallback for macOS IDA 9.4+ where `sys.executable` is idat itself.
86	
87	**What breaks:**
88	- Version mismatch: User can set this to a Python 3.14 venv while idapyswitch registered libpython3.12. IDA loads 3.12 but packages are for 3.14. HCLI warns about this in `explain-environment` but not during normal operations (#278).
89	- If the path doesn't exist (stale env var), HCLI falls through to the idat probe.
90	- Not documented anywhere in official IDA docs.
91	
92	**Prevalence:** Growing — the recommended approach, but adoption limited by lack of documentation.
93	
94	## 7. HCLI_CURRENT_IDA_PYTHON_EXE environment variable (bypass)
95	
96	**What the user does:** Sets `HCLI_CURRENT_IDA_PYTHON_EXE` to point directly at the Python executable HCLI should use. This is an HCLI-specific escape hatch, not an IDA config.
97	
98	**How HCLI discovers it:** `resolve_current_python()` checks this first, before everything else. If set, returns it immediately with no validation — no probe, no existence check, no version check.
99	
100	**What breaks:**
101	- No validation at all — if the path is wrong, HCLI will fail later with confusing errors.
102	- No probe data available, so version mismatch detection can't run.
103	- This is a workaround, not a proper setup — the error message from probe failures suggests it.
104	
105	**Prevalence:** Rare — used in CI pipelines or when troubleshooting probe failures.
106	
107	## 8. uv venv without --seed
108	
109	**What the user does:** Creates a venv with `uv venv ~/.idapro/venv` (without `--seed`). This creates a minimal venv that does NOT include pip.
110	
111	**How HCLI discovers it:** Discovered normally (via env var or probe), but when HCLI tries to install packages with `pip`, it fails.
112	
113	**What breaks:**
114	- `PipNotAvailableError` because pip is not installed (#124).
115	- User must learn to use `uv venv --seed` or install pip manually.
116	
117	**Prevalence:** Occasional — users familiar with uv but not with IDA's pip requirement.
118	
119	## 9. uv run --with ida-hcli (ephemeral overlay)
120	
121	**What the user does:** Runs `uv run --with ida-hcli hcli <command>` instead of installing HCLI. uv creates an ephemeral cache environment with HCLI and its deps, and sets `$VIRTUAL_ENV` to point at it.
122	
123	**How HCLI discovers it:** `is_uv_cache_virtual_env()` detects the overlay using three heuristics:
124	1. Path is under a known uv cache dir (`~/.cache/uv/`, etc.)
125	2. Path has uv-internal ancestor dirs (`archive-v0/`, `builds-v0/`)
126	3. `pyvenv.cfg` contains `extends-environment` key (uv 0.7.9+)
127	
128	When detected, `resolve_user_virtual_env()` scans `$PATH` for the real user venv.
129	
130	**What breaks:**
131	- The real user venv is hidden behind uv's overlay. If HCLI can't find it via PATH scanning, it falls back to the system Python.
132	- The uv cache venv is HCLI's own process environment, not IDA's — installing there would be useless.
133	
134	**Prevalence:** Occasional — users who prefer not to install HCLI globally.
135	
136	## 10. Conda/Anaconda environment
137	
138	**What the user does:** Creates a conda environment, installs Python there, uses `idapyswitch` to point IDA at the conda env's libpython.
139	
140	**How HCLI discovers it:** Via the standard idat probe. IDA 9.4 added detection for Anaconda Pythons. `sys.prefix` points into the conda env.
141	
142	**What breaks:**
143	- Conda environments are not standard venvs — they don't have `pyvenv.cfg`, which HCLI uses for venv detection.
144	- `is_uv_cache_virtual_env()` and `_get_venv_root_from_python()` won't recognize conda envs.
145	- Package management confusion: conda install vs. pip install.
146	
147	**Prevalence:** Uncommon for IDA, more common in data science adjacent use cases.
148	
149	## 11. IDAEnvOrchestrator or similar third-party tools
150	
151	**What the user does:** Uses a community tool (e.g., IDAEnvOrchestrator by quippy-dev) that automates virtualenv/conda detection and path patching in `idapythonrc.py`.
152	
153	**How HCLI discovers it:** Depends on what the tool sets up. If it activates a venv via `idapythonrc.py`, HCLI has the same visibility gap as variant #5. If it sets `IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE`, HCLI picks it up directly.
154	
155	**What breaks:** Same issues as whichever underlying mechanism the tool uses.
156	
157	**Prevalence:** Rare.
158	
159	## 12. No Python configured at all
160	
161	**What the user does:** IDA is installed on a system without Python, or Python is installed but idapyswitch was never run to register it.
162	
163	**How HCLI discovers it:** The idat probe fails (IDA can't start its embedded Python, or returns `frozen: true`). `resolve_current_python()` raises `PythonNotFoundError` with guidance to set `HCLI_CURRENT_IDA_PYTHON_EXE`.
164	
165	**What breaks:** Everything — no Python environment probing, no plugin installation. IDA 9.4 added "don't crash on launch when Python is not configured" but HCLI still can't do anything.
166	
167	**Prevalence:** Rare but reported (#85 — failures when default IDA installation isn't registered).
168	
169	## Summary: The Resolution Precedence Chain
170	
171	`resolve_current_python()` in python.py checks in this order:
172	1. `$HCLI_CURRENT_IDA_PYTHON_EXE` → trust blindly, return immediately
173	2. `$IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE` → if file exists on disk, return immediately
174	3. idat probe → spawn IDA, run probe script, then `_derive_python_exe()`:
175	   a. Build candidates from `sys.prefix`/`sys.base_prefix` with platform-specific paths
176	   b. Match candidates against `$IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE` venv root
177	   c. Match candidates against `$VIRTUAL_ENV`
178	   d. Accept any existing candidate when prefix ≠ base_prefix (venv detected)
179	   e. Validate `sys.executable` against `$IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE` venv root
180	   f. Validate `sys.executable` against `$VIRTUAL_ENV`
181	   g. Match `sys.executable` against `$IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE` directly
182	   h. Trust `$IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE` directly (IDA 9.4+ macOS fallback)
183	   i. Accept any existing prefix candidate (final fallback)
184	   j. Raise `PythonNotFoundError`
185	
186	## Environment Variables That Affect Python Resolution
187	
188	| Variable | Source | Effect |
189	|---|---|---|
190	| `HCLI_CURRENT_IDA_PYTHON_EXE` | HCLI | Bypass all detection, use this Python directly |
191	| `IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE` | IDAPython (9.1+) | Point at venv interpreter; skips idat probe when file exists |
192	| `VIRTUAL_ENV` | Shell activation | Used by idat probe to validate venv candidates; can be hijacked by uv overlays |
193	| `PYTHONHOME` | Python | Scrubbed by HCLI before launching idat to prevent env leakage |
194	| `PYTHONPATH` | Python | Can leak into idat subprocess and cause wrong module loading |
195	| `UV_CACHE_DIR` | uv | Used to detect uv cache environments |
196

- PEP 668: On Ubuntu 24.04+, Debian, and some macOS, the system Python is marked `EXTERNALLY-MANAGED` and pip refuses to install anything (#275, #144).
- Permission errors: System Python environments may be in read-only locations (`/usr/lib/python3/...`).
- Windows Store shims: PATH lookup finds `python3.EXE` in `Microsoft\WindowsApps` which opens the Store instead of running Python (#154). HCLI now detects and rejects these via `_is_windows_store_shim()`.
- `sys.executable` is `idat.exe` on Windows (#133) and on macOS IDA 9.4+ — HCLI can't trust it.
- No writable environment for plugin dependencies.

**Prevalence:** Very common — the default for most users, especially new ones.

## 2. Windows bundled Python

**What the user does:** Runs the IDA installer on Windows with `--install_python` (or accepts the default to bundle Python 3). IDA ships with a private Python installation in the IDA directory.

**How HCLI discovers it:** Same as (1): idat probe finds the bundled interpreter via `sys.prefix`. The path is typically inside the IDA installation directory.

**What breaks:**
- The bundled Python is not a venv, so it may lack pip or have restricted permissions depending on where IDA is installed (e.g., `C:\Program Files\...`).
- No isolation from other IDA installations or system Python.
- Users may not realize they have two Pythons (bundled + system) and get confused about which one IDA uses.

**Prevalence:** Common on Windows, especially for users who accept installer defaults.

## 3. Homebrew / pyenv / Anaconda / system-installed Python via idapyswitch

**What the user does:** Installs Python via Homebrew (`brew install python`), pyenv, Anaconda/Miniconda, or python.org installer. Runs `idapyswitch` to point IDA at that Python's `libpython3.X.dylib/.so/.dll`.

**How HCLI discovers it:** The idat probe reports the Homebrew/pyenv/Anaconda prefix as `sys.prefix`. HCLI derives the executable from that prefix. IDA 9.4 added detection for uv/anaconda/homebrew Pythons.

**What breaks:**
- No venv means package installation affects the global environment.
- Homebrew Python on macOS may be externally managed (PEP 668).
- Anaconda environments add another layer of complexity (conda envs vs. Python venvs).
- pyenv shims can confuse PATH-based fallback detection.
- macOS framework Pythons report misleading `sys.base_prefix` values, causing HCLI to miss the venv when one is active.

**Prevalence:** Common among power users and macOS users.

## 4. Virtual environment activated via shell before launching IDA

**What the user does:** Creates a venv (`python -m venv ~/.idapro/venv` or `uv venv --seed ~/.idapro/venv`), activates it in the shell (`source ~/.idapro/venv/bin/activate`), then launches IDA from that shell. IDA 9.0+ picks up locally installed modules from the activated venv.

**How HCLI discovers it:** The idat probe sees `$VIRTUAL_ENV` set and `sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix`. HCLI's `_derive_python_exe` matches prefix candidates against `$VIRTUAL_ENV` to find the correct interpreter inside the venv.

**What breaks:**
- Only works when IDA is launched from the activated shell. Doesn't work with desktop shortcuts, file associations, or system launchers.
- If HCLI is invoked separately (not from the same activated shell), it won't see `$VIRTUAL_ENV`.
- The 9.0 release notes describe this as "simply run IDA from an activated virtual environment" — one sentence, no further guidance.

**Prevalence:** Uncommon — inconvenient for daily use, mainly used by developers and CI.

## 5. Virtual environment activated via idapythonrc.py

**What the user does:** Creates a venv, then adds activation code to `~/.idapro/idapythonrc.py`. The script uses `site.addsitedir()` to add the venv's `site-packages` to `sys.path` and sets `sys.prefix` to the venv root. Runs at every IDA startup.

Community-recommended approaches (from https://community.hex-rays.com/t/using-a-virtualenv-for-idapython/261):
- Original: Uses `activate_this.py` from the `virtualenv` package (not stdlib `venv`).
- Improved (mrexodia): Uses a sentinel flag in `builtins` to prevent re-initialization when switching databases, directly manages site-packages via `site.addsitedir()`.

**How HCLI discovers it:** This is where the gap is. HCLI's batch-mode idat probe (`idat -A -S<script>`) does NOT trigger `idapythonrc.py` the same way interactive IDA does (depends on `IDA_IS_INTERACTIVE`). So the probe sees the base system Python while interactive IDA uses the venv (#144). HCLI may install packages into the wrong location.

If `$VIRTUAL_ENV` happens to also be set (because the user activated the venv in their shell), HCLI may pick it up from the probe results. But this is unreliable.

**What breaks:**
- HCLI cannot see the venv — it installs packages into the wrong Python.
- `activate_this.py` only exists in `virtualenv`-created envs, not stdlib `venv` or `uv venv`.
- Script may execute multiple times per process when opening multiple databases.
- `idapythonrc.py` is completely undocumented in official IDA docs.

**Prevalence:** Common — the most-recommended community approach before `IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE` existed.

## 6. IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE environment variable (recommended)

**What the user does:** Creates a venv, then sets `IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE` as a persistent environment variable pointing to the venv's Python interpreter (e.g., `~/.idapro/venv/bin/python3`). Available since IDA 9.1+.

**How HCLI discovers it:** `resolve_current_python()` checks `ENV.IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE` as second priority (after `HCLI_CURRENT_IDA_PYTHON_EXE`). If the file exists on disk, returns it immediately — no idat probe needed. Inside the idat probe, `_derive_python_exe` also uses it to validate candidates and as a direct fallback for macOS IDA 9.4+ where `sys.executable` is idat itself.

**What breaks:**
- Version mismatch: User can set this to a Python 3.14 venv while idapyswitch registered libpython3.12. IDA loads 3.12 but packages are for 3.14. HCLI warns about this in `explain-environment` but not during normal operations (#278).
- If the path doesn't exist (stale env var), HCLI falls through to the idat probe.
- Not documented anywhere in official IDA docs.

**Prevalence:** Growing — the recommended approach, but adoption limited by lack of documentation.

## 7. HCLI_CURRENT_IDA_PYTHON_EXE environment variable (bypass)

**What the user does:** Sets `HCLI_CURRENT_IDA_PYTHON_EXE` to point directly at the Python executable HCLI should use. This is an HCLI-specific escape hatch, not an IDA config.

**How HCLI discovers it:** `resolve_current_python()` checks this first, before everything else. If set, returns it immediately with no validation — no probe, no existence check, no version check.

**What breaks:**
- No validation at all — if the path is wrong, HCLI will fail later with confusing errors.
- No probe data available, so version mismatch detection can't run.
- This is a workaround, not a proper setup — the error message from probe failures suggests it.

**Prevalence:** Rare — used in CI pipelines or when troubleshooting probe failures.

## 8. uv venv without --seed

**What the user does:** Creates a venv with `uv venv ~/.idapro/venv` (without `--seed`). This creates a minimal venv that does NOT include pip.

**How HCLI discovers it:** Discovered normally (via env var or probe), but when HCLI tries to install packages with `pip`, it fails.

**What breaks:**
- `PipNotAvailableError` because pip is not installed (#124).
- User must learn to use `uv venv --seed` or install pip manually.

**Prevalence:** Occasional — users familiar with uv but not with IDA's pip requirement.

## 9. uv run --with ida-hcli (ephemeral overlay)

**What the user does:** Runs `uv run --with ida-hcli hcli <command>` instead of installing HCLI. uv creates an ephemeral cache environment with HCLI and its deps, and sets `$VIRTUAL_ENV` to point at it.

**How HCLI discovers it:** `is_uv_cache_virtual_env()` detects the overlay using three heuristics:
1. Path is under a known uv cache dir (`~/.cache/uv/`, etc.)
2. Path has uv-internal ancestor dirs (`archive-v0/`, `builds-v0/`)
3. `pyvenv.cfg` contains `extends-environment` key (uv 0.7.9+)

When detected, `resolve_user_virtual_env()` scans `$PATH` for the real user venv.

**What breaks:**
- The real user venv is hidden behind uv's overlay. If HCLI can't find it via PATH scanning, it falls back to the system Python.
- The uv cache venv is HCLI's own process environment, not IDA's — installing there would be useless.

**Prevalence:** Occasional — users who prefer not to install HCLI globally.

## 10. Conda/Anaconda environment

**What the user does:** Creates a conda environment, installs Python there, uses `idapyswitch` to point IDA at the conda env's libpython.

**How HCLI discovers it:** Via the standard idat probe. IDA 9.4 added detection for Anaconda Pythons. `sys.prefix` points into the conda env.

**What breaks:**
- Conda environments are not standard venvs — they don't have `pyvenv.cfg`, which HCLI uses for venv detection.
- `is_uv_cache_virtual_env()` and `_get_venv_root_from_python()` won't recognize conda envs.
- Package management confusion: conda install vs. pip install.

**Prevalence:** Uncommon for IDA, more common in data science adjacent use cases.

## 11. IDAEnvOrchestrator or similar third-party tools

**What the user does:** Uses a community tool (e.g., IDAEnvOrchestrator by quippy-dev) that automates virtualenv/conda detection and path patching in `idapythonrc.py`.

**How HCLI discovers it:** Depends on what the tool sets up. If it activates a venv via `idapythonrc.py`, HCLI has the same visibility gap as variant #5. If it sets `IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE`, HCLI picks it up directly.

**What breaks:** Same issues as whichever underlying mechanism the tool uses.

**Prevalence:** Rare.

## 12. No Python configured at all

**What the user does:** IDA is installed on a system without Python, or Python is installed but idapyswitch was never run to register it.

**How HCLI discovers it:** The idat probe fails (IDA can't start its embedded Python, or returns `frozen: true`). `resolve_current_python()` raises `PythonNotFoundError` with guidance to set `HCLI_CURRENT_IDA_PYTHON_EXE`.

**What breaks:** Everything — no Python environment probing, no plugin installation. IDA 9.4 added "don't crash on launch when Python is not configured" but HCLI still can't do anything.

**Prevalence:** Rare but reported (#85 — failures when default IDA installation isn't registered).

## Summary: The Resolution Precedence Chain

`resolve_current_python()` in python.py checks in this order:
1. `$HCLI_CURRENT_IDA_PYTHON_EXE` → trust blindly, return immediately
2. `$IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE` → if file exists on disk, return immediately
3. idat probe → spawn IDA, run probe script, then `_derive_python_exe()`:
   a. Build candidates from `sys.prefix`/`sys.base_prefix` with platform-specific paths
   b. Match candidates against `$IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE` venv root
   c. Match candidates against `$VIRTUAL_ENV`
   d. Accept any existing candidate when prefix ≠ base_prefix (venv detected)
   e. Validate `sys.executable` against `$IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE` venv root
   f. Validate `sys.executable` against `$VIRTUAL_ENV`
   g. Match `sys.executable` against `$IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE` directly
   h. Trust `$IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE` directly (IDA 9.4+ macOS fallback)
   i. Accept any existing prefix candidate (final fallback)
   j. Raise `PythonNotFoundError`

## Environment Variables That Affect Python Resolution

| Variable | Source | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `HCLI_CURRENT_IDA_PYTHON_EXE` | HCLI | Bypass all detection, use this Python directly |
| `IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE` | IDAPython (9.1+) | Point at venv interpreter; skips idat probe when file exists |
| `VIRTUAL_ENV` | Shell activation | Used by idat probe to validate venv candidates; can be hijacked by uv overlays |
| `PYTHONHOME` | Python | Scrubbed by HCLI before launching idat to prevent env leakage |
| `PYTHONPATH` | Python | Can leak into idat subprocess and cause wrong module loading |
| `UV_CACHE_DIR` | uv | Used to detect uv cache environments |

Setting `IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE` is the key change. It lets HCLI skip the idat probe entirely, which eliminates the 3-5 second startup penalty, makes IDA Home and IDA Free editions work (no `idat` needed), and makes the env var visible to HCLI regardless of how IDA itself activates the venv via `idapythonrc.py`. The env var is also easy to set in GitHub Actions and Docker containers.

## Non-recommended setups

Users arrive at many different Python configurations depending on their OS, how they installed IDA, and what advice they found online. Each of the following setups is something users actually do today, and each has problems that the recommended setup avoids.

**System Python with no virtual environment.** This is the default for most users: install IDA, do nothing about Python. On Linux/macOS, IDA uses whatever system Python `idapyswitch` finds. On Windows, the installer can bundle a private Python via `--install_python`. In both cases the Python environment is not writable by HCLI for package installation. On Ubuntu 24.04+ and Debian, pip refuses to install anything because the system Python is marked externally-managed (PEP 668). On Windows, `sys.executable` inside IDA reports `idat.exe` rather than the Python interpreter, and PATH-based fallback can find the Windows Store shim instead of the real Python. This is the most common setup and the source of most support requests.

**Homebrew, pyenv, or Anaconda Python via idapyswitch.** Power users (especially on macOS) install Python through a package manager, then run `idapyswitch` to register that Python's `libpython` with IDA. Without a venv, package installation still affects the global environment. Homebrew Python on macOS may also be PEP 668 externally-managed. Anaconda environments are not standard venvs (no `pyvenv.cfg`), so HCLI's venv detection does not recognize them. pyenv shims can confuse PATH-based fallback. macOS framework Pythons report misleading `sys.base_prefix` values, causing HCLI to misidentify the interpreter.

**Shell-activated venv.** The user creates a venv, activates it in their shell, and launches IDA from that shell. IDA 9.0+ picks up modules from the activated venv. The 9.0 release notes describe this as "simply run IDA from an activated virtual environment." This only works when IDA is launched from an activated terminal session. Desktop shortcuts, file associations, and system launchers don't carry the shell activation, so IDA reverts to the base Python. When HCLI is invoked from a different terminal, it won't see `$VIRTUAL_ENV` either.

**`idapythonrc.py` venv activation.** Before `IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE` existed, the community-recommended approach was to add venv activation code to `~/.idapro/idapythonrc.py`. A [Hex-Rays community post](https://community.hex-rays.com/t/using-a-virtualenv-for-idapython/261) describes the technique: use `site.addsitedir()` to inject the venv's `site-packages` into `sys.path` at IDA startup. This works for interactive IDA, but HCLI's batch-mode probe (`idat -A -S<script>`) does not execute `idapythonrc.py` the same way. The probe sees the base system Python while interactive IDA uses the venv. Users confirm their setup works inside IDA, yet HCLI installs packages into the wrong location. The `idapythonrc.py` file itself is not mentioned anywhere in the official IDA documentation.

**`uv venv` without `--seed`.** Users familiar with `uv` create a venv with `uv venv ~/.idapro/venv` but omit the `--seed` flag. The resulting venv has no pip installed. HCLI finds the correct Python but fails with `PipNotAvailableError` when it tries to install plugin dependencies. The fix is to use `uv venv --seed` or to install pip manually, but this is not obvious from the error message.

**`uv run --with ida-hcli` (ephemeral overlay).** Users who prefer not to install HCLI globally run `uv run --with ida-hcli hcli <command>`. This causes `uv` to create an ephemeral cache environment and set `$VIRTUAL_ENV` to point at it, hiding the user's actual IDA venv. HCLI has three heuristics to detect these overlays (path under uv cache dirs, uv-internal ancestor directory names, `extends-environment` key in `pyvenv.cfg`), but if detection fails, HCLI installs into the ephemeral environment which is discarded after the command exits.

**No Python configured.** On systems where Python is not installed, or where `idapyswitch` was never run, IDA starts without IDAPython. IDA 9.4 no longer crashes in this case, but HCLI's probe fails entirely and no plugin operations are possible.

The recommended setup (`IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE` pointing at a properly versioned venv with pip) avoids every one of these failure modes. It also provides a single, verifiable state that HCLI can check without spawning IDA.

## Current state of IDA documentation

The official documentation at [docs.hex-rays.com](https://docs.hex-rays.com/) provides almost no guidance on Python configuration. A user who reads every relevant page will learn very little about how to set up Python for IDA. What follows is a complete audit of every reference to IDAPython configuration across the documentation, conducted 2026-09-09 against IDA 9.4-era docs.

The [installation page](https://docs.hex-rays.com/getting-started/install-ida.md) says "Make sure Python 3 or later is installed on your computer for the IDAPython API to function properly" and nothing else about Python. This sentence is identical across macOS, Linux, and Windows sections. It does not say which Python, how to verify it, or what happens with multiple Python installations. The [installer command-line options](https://docs.hex-rays.com/getting-started/install-ida/ida-installer-commandline-options.md) page documents a Windows-only `--install_python` flag to bundle Python 3, and notes "On Linux and Mac, the system-wide Python is presumed to be available."

The [IDAPython landing page](https://docs.hex-rays.com/developer/idapython.md), [getting started guide](https://docs.hex-rays.com/developer/idapython/idapython-getting-started.md), and [how-tos](https://docs.hex-rays.com/developer/idapython/how-tos.md) cover the API (modules, constants, code snippets, plugin structure) but contain no information about interpreter selection, virtual environments, pip, or environment setup.

The [plugin publishing guide](https://docs.hex-rays.com/developer/publishing-plugins/how-tos/plugin-publishing.md) documents the `pythonDependencies` field in `ida-plugin.json` and states that "HCLI automatically places plugins in the correct locations, installs required Python dependencies, and handles additional setup tasks." It does not explain what happens when that automatic installation fails (PEP 668, missing pip, wrong Python) or what the user should do about it.

The [environment variables page](https://docs.hex-rays.com/core/disassembler/concepts/environment-variables.md) lists ~35 IDA environment variables. None are Python-related. `IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE`, `PYTHONPATH`, `VIRTUAL_ENV`, and `IDAPYSWITCH` are all absent. The [configuration files page](https://docs.hex-rays.com/core/user-interface/concepts/configuration-files.md) lists `IDAPYTHON.CFG` as a config file but provides no details about its contents, location, or usage. The [troubleshooting pages](https://docs.hex-rays.com/core/user-interface/troubleshooting.md) cover disassembly/analysis issues only, with no Python-related entries.

The [idalib getting started guide](https://docs.hex-rays.com/core/idalib/getting-started.md) shows `uv pip install idapro` and running `py-activate-idalib.py`, making it the closest the docs come to showing Python environment management. But this is specific to idalib and doesn't discuss the IDA desktop application's Python configuration.

Release notes contain more Python environment information than the documentation itself. The [IDA 9.0 release notes](https://docs.hex-rays.com/release-notes/9_0.md) announce: "Python virtual environments (venvs) are now supported - simply run IDA from an activated virtual environment and it will pick up locally installed modules." This is the only place in the entire documentation that mentions venv support, and the guidance is one sentence. It does not explain how to create the venv, what "activated" means in this context, how `idapyswitch` interacts with venvs, or what `IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE` is. The same release notes mention that `idapyswitch` can now function "with read-only IDA installations" and can "detect recent homebrew versions on macOS." The [IDA 9.4 release notes](https://docs.hex-rays.com/release-notes/9_4.md) add one-line changelog entries for "detect/support pythons managed by uv/anaconda/homebrew," "warn on libpython/venv version mismatch," and "don't crash on launch when Python is not configured," with no explanation of what users should do in each case.

The following topics are absent from the documentation: `idapyswitch` has no documentation page and appears only in changelog lines. `IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE` is not mentioned anywhere. `idapythonrc.py` is not mentioned anywhere; users discover it from [community forums](https://community.hex-rays.com/t/using-a-virtualenv-for-idapython/261) or IDA's sample files. There is no page explaining how to create a virtual environment for IDA, what Python version to use, where to put it, or how to register it. The requirement that the venv Python version must match the `libpython` registered with `idapyswitch` is not documented. There is no explanation of how to install Python packages into IDA's environment, and no troubleshooting guide for PEP 668, externally-managed environments, wrong Python detection, or common error messages.

The official documentation at [docs.hex-rays.com](https://docs.hex-rays.com/) provides almost no guidance on Python configuration. The [plugin publishing guide](https://docs.hex-rays.com/developer/publishing-plugins/how-tos/plugin-publishing.md) documents the `pythonDependencies` field in `ida-plugin.json` and states that "HCLI automatically places plugins in the correct locations, installs required Python dependencies, and handles additional setup tasks." It does not explain what happens when that automatic installation fails (PEP 668, missing pip, wrong Python) or what the user should do about it.

The [environment variables page](https://docs.hex-rays.com/core/disassembler/concepts/environment-variables.md) lists ~35 IDA environment variables. None are Python-related. `IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE`, `PYTHONPATH`, `VIRTUAL_ENV`, and `IDAPYSWITCH` are all absent. The [configuration files page](https://docs.hex-rays.com/core/user-interface/concepts/configuration-files.md) lists `IDAPYTHON.CFG` as a config file but provides no details about its contents, location, or usage. The [troubleshooting pages](https://docs.hex-rays.com/core/user-interface/troubleshooting.md) cover disassembly/analysis issues only, with no Python-related entries.

The [idalib getting started guide](https://docs.hex-rays.com/core/idalib/getting-started.md) shows `uv pip install idapro` and running `py-activate-idalib.py`, making it the closest the docs come to showing Python environment management. But this is specific to idalib and doesn't discuss the IDA desktop application's Python configuration.

Release notes contain more Python environment information than the documentation itself. The [IDA 9.0 release notes](https://docs.hex-rays.com/release-notes/9_0.md) announce: "Python virtual environments (venvs) are now supported - simply run IDA from an activated virtual environment and it will pick up locally installed modules." This is the only place in the entire documentation that mentions venv support, and the guidance is one sentence. It does not explain how to create the venv, what "activated" means in this context, how `idapyswitch` interacts with venvs, or what `IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE` is. The same release notes mention that `idapyswitch` can now function "with read-only IDA installations" and can "detect recent homebrew versions on macOS." The [IDA 9.4 release notes](https://docs.hex-rays.com/release-notes/9_4.md) add one-line changelog entries for "detect/support pythons managed by uv/anaconda/homebrew," "warn on libpython/venv version mismatch," and "don't crash on launch when Python is not configured," with no explanation of what users should do in each case.

The following topics are absent from the documentation: `idapyswitch` has no documentation page and appears only in changelog lines. `IDAPYTHON_VENV_EXECUTABLE` is not mentioned anywhere. `idapythonrc.py` is not mentioned anywhere; users discover it from [community forums](https://community.hex-rays.com/t/using-a-virtualenv-for-idapython/261) or IDA's sample files. There is no page explaining how to create a virtual environment for IDA, what Python version to use, where to put it, or how to register it. The requirement that the venv Python version must match the `libpython` registered with `idapyswitch` is not documented. There is no explanation of how to install Python packages into IDA's environment, and no troubleshooting guide for PEP 668, externally-managed environments, wrong Python detection, or common error messages.
